title: What are NPM and Yarn?
description: Understand what a package manager does, how npm, Yarn, and pnpm differ, and how to pin one per repository.

data.text: A **package manager** installs, updates, and removes the libraries your project depends on. npm ships with Node.js, Yarn was created at Facebook to make installs faster and deterministic, and pnpm later optimised disk usage with a content-addressable store.
What a package manager actually does

Every `npm install` performs the same four steps: it reads `package.json`, resolves a dependency graph against the registry, downloads and extracts tarballs, then writes a **lockfile** so the next install produces an identical tree. Binaries are linked into `node_modules/.bin`, which is why `npx` and `npm run` can find tools like `eslint` without a global install.
The commands you will type every day

data.title: The same task in all three managers
data.content: Install a dependency, then replay the install from a lockfile in CI.
data.code:
npm install express
npm ci

# Yarn
yarn add express
yarn install --immutable

# pnpm
pnpm add express
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

data.title: One manager per repository
data.text: Mixing managers is the most common cause of "works on my machine" bugs. Two lockfiles mean two different dependency trees, and whichever is committed last wins. Delete the unused lockfile and add a `packageManager` field so everyone uses the same version.

Corepack is bundled with modern Node.js and reads the `packageManager` field. Run `corepack enable` once, and the exact npm, Yarn, or pnpm version recorded in `package.json` is downloaded and used automatically — the same version in every developer shell and on CI.

data.title: Enable Corepack and switch versions
data.content: After this, the pinned Yarn version is used even if a different one is installed globally.
data.code:
corepack enable
corepack use yarn@4.5.0
corepack use pnpm@9.12.0   # reads and rewrites packageManager

terms.definition: A server that hosts packages — by default https://registry.npmjs.org.
A generated file that pins the exact version and integrity hash of every dependency, so installs are reproducible.
The directory where resolved packages are extracted and made importable.
The Node.js shim that installs and runs the package manager version declared in packageManager.

data.caption: How an install turns package.json into a runnable node_modules
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[package.json] --> B[Resolve dependency graph]
    B --> C[Registry]
    C --> D[Download tarballs]
    D --> E[Write lockfile]
    D --> F[node_modules and .bin links]
    E --> G[npm ci / yarn install --immutable]

items.question: Which manager should I pick for a new project?
items.answer: npm if you want zero setup and maximum compatibility; pnpm or Yarn if install speed, strictness, and monorepo tooling matter. What matters most is that the whole team commits to one.

items.question: Can I migrate an existing project between managers?
items.answer: Yes. Delete node_modules and the old lockfile, then run the new manager install once. Review the new lockfile in the pull request — resolution differences occasionally surface real version conflicts.

items.question: Do I commit node_modules?
items.answer: No. Commit the lockfile instead. Exceptions are rare (for example offline deployments without registry access).

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Every manager resolves a graph, writes a lockfile, and links binaries into node_modules/.bin.
npm, Yarn, and pnpm differ mainly in install model and strictness — not in what they can install.
Commit exactly one lockfile and pin the manager with packageManager plus Corepack.
Use the frozen/immutable install command (npm ci) in CI, never npm install.
data.takeaway: If you can explain the lockfile and why CI uses a frozen install, you can answer most package-manager interview questions.
